case_study_insert.main_stem: Harrowgate Riverside Inns (HRI) is a public limited company in the hospitality and riverside dining sector, employing a workforce of 230. Founded in 1987 by Margaret Harrowgate, the group operates nine riverside inns across the county, with a hierarchical structure and autocratic leadership. HRI plans to invest $1,800,000 in refurbishing six inns with riverside dining terraces and boutique rooms, financed by a $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $1,140,000 a year, a variable cost of $38 a unit and a selling price of $95, and currently produces 26,000 units a year. HRI faces two operational problems: labour turnover has reached 28% in its kitchens and food-waste complaints at two inns are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Autumn 2025: Customer complaints across the nine inns fell from 44 to 27 per month, and food waste is running at 9.5% of kitchen preparation weight. Average room occupancy is 71%, and the 600 most recent guest reviews average 4.2 out of 5. Market research of 700 diners found that 55% would pay up to $8 more for locally sourced riverside menus, and 46% check ingredient provenance before booking. Off-the-job food hygiene courses at the county college cost $480 per employee for the 160 kitchen and service staff.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Harrowgate Riverside Inns as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.5%, the fourth rise this year, increasing costs for variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.30 to $13.09 per hour from April 2026, raising kitchen and service wage bills. (3) Food and beverage input costs have risen 13.1% year-on-year, leisure inflation is running at 7.9%, and consumer spending on eating out grew 2.6% in the same period.

questions.question_text: HRI plans to finance its six-inn refurbishment partly with a $600,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for HRI of using a share issue instead of a larger bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue raises capital without creating a repayment obligation, so HRI's cash flow is not strained by fixed monthly repayments while the refurbishment disrupts six inns. Unlike the $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan, new equity carries no interest charge, protecting fixed costs of $1,140,000 a year and freeing cash to absorb the 13.1% rise in food and beverage input costs without raising menu prices above the $95 room-night benchmark.

Point 2: Equity funding strengthens HRI's statement of financial position, lowering the burden on its current ratio and leaving capacity to borrow again if terrace costs overrun. It also spreads ownership and risk across more shareholders rather than concentrating debt with one bank, which suits a public limited company refurbishing $1,800,000 of assets, and avoids covenants that could restrict how the inns are operated during the refit.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Harrowgate Riverside Inns and its refurbishment decision.

questions.question_text: HRI is relaunching its six refurbished riverside inns. Consider a county-wide television advertising campaign, food and travel magazine print features, or a social media campaign with regional food critics and influencers. Which should HRI choose to promote the relaunch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
County-wide television advertising: TV would deliver rapid mass awareness of the terraces and boutique rooms across the region and could be timed to the summer eating season. However, production and airtime costs are very high, much of the county audience never visits these particular inns, and the spend is hard to attribute to bookings for a group already trading at 71% occupancy.

Magazine print features: Long-lead features in food and travel magazines would reach an affluent, food-focused readership that values riverside setting and locally sourced menus — exactly the 55% of 700 surveyed diners willing to pay up to $8 more, and the 46% who check provenance. Print is tangible and prestigious, but readership is skewing older, placement costs are significant, and results arrive slowly.

Food-critic and influencer social campaign: Partnering with regional food critics and lifestyle influencers produces trackable, appetising content that showcases the terraces and locally sourced menus, reaching younger diners who book weekend breaks. Costs are flexible and engagement measurable, though credibility depends on critic honesty and results build more slowly than broadcast.

Recommendation: HRI should choose the food-critic and influencer social campaign. It targets the provenance-conscious 46% and the 55% willing to pay the premium most directly, costs far less than county TV, scales beyond print readership, and suits the 4.2-out-of-5 review base HRI already holds. County television is rejected as unaffordable and weakly targeted for nine inns; magazine features are rejected as too slow and narrow for a relaunch that needs momentum within one season, and can be used later as supporting PR.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal application to HRI.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of HRI with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of HRI with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and print are rejected.

questions.question_text: HRI must maintain consistency in its kitchens during the refurbishment. Explain two benefits for HRI of using autocratic leadership to improve kitchen performance and reliability.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership gives HRI's kitchen brigade clear, immediate direction from head chefs on recipes, portioning and hygiene, which is critical while six inns are refitted and standards risk drifting. Decisive command reduces errors that feed food-waste complaints, helping reverse the rise at two inns and protecting the 4.2 out of 5 review average.

Point 2: In a hierarchical structure, autocratic decisions cascade quickly through clear chains of command, so new menus and terrace service rules are adopted uniformly across nine inns without lengthy consultation. For relatively inexperienced seasonal kitchen staff this consistency raises output per worker and lowers the risk of service failures, cutting the 28% kitchen labour turnover caused by unclear expectations and reducing the need to re-recruit and retrain against the $480 per employee food hygiene course cost.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HRI's kitchens, refurbishment and review scores.

questions.question_text: HRI needs a head chef for its flagship riverside terrace. Consider recruiting an experienced head chef externally, or promoting and training the sous-chef from within the group. Which should HRI choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External recruitment: An external head chef brings fresh fine-dining techniques, terrace-showcooking experience and possibly a following from a previous restaurant, which could lift occupancy above 71% and justify the $8 premium diners say they will pay. However, top chefs command premium salaries and relocation, recruitment takes months, and an outsider may clash with HRI's hierarchical kitchen culture and existing 160-strong brigade.

Internal promotion of the sous-chef: Promoting the sous-chef from within rewards loyalty, preserves knowledge of HRI's menus and suppliers, and signals a clear career path that can motivate the brigade and reduce the 28% kitchen labour turnover. The promoted chef will need structured training — for example off-the-job management courses at $480 per head plus menu-development mentoring — and may lack fine-dining terrace theatre experience.

Decision: HRI should promote and train the sous-chef, supported by short external masterclasses and a trial terrace residency. Internal promotion is cheaper, faster and culturally aligned, protects the falling 27-per-month complaint rate, and strengthens retention across nine inns. Full external recruitment is rejected because premium salary costs and cultural disruption are hard to justify when HRI already holds a capable number two, and any skill gap can be closed with targeted off-the-job training within months.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to HRI.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of HRI.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of HRI with a well-justified decision covering cost, culture, retention and menu quality.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how HRI's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $1,140,000 ÷ ($95 − $38) = $1,140,000 ÷ $57 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $95 − $38 = $57.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $57.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways HRI's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 20,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 26,000 units to confirm the inn group is profitably above break-even, with a margin of safety of 6,000 units, informing whether the six refurbished terraces can absorb the nine-inn fixed cost base.
2. Contribution per unit of $57.00 lets HRI model the locally sourced menu uplift, for example a $8 premium menu maintaining a $95 price would hold contribution at $57.00 while raising volume, letting managers judge whether provenance marketing covers the extra $38 variable cost.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $1,140,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the occupancy and cover targets used to justify the $1,200,000 bank loan repayments, and to check the terraces service them before drawing on the $600,000 share-issue programme.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($1,140,000 ÷ 26,000 units + $38 = $81.85 a unit) to benchmark inn-by-inn performance, identify kitchen waste behind the 9.5% of prep weight, and decide whether to renegotiate the $38 variable cost with food suppliers amid the 13.1% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $57.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 26,000-unit output; locally sourced menu modelling vs $1,140,000 fixed costs; loan-repayment feasibility for the $1,800,000 refurbishment; and unit-cost benchmarking at $81.85 to tackle the 9.5% food waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate HRI's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has HRI's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.60 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.08 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.16 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $210,000 inventories + $320,000 trade receivables + $110,000 cash = $640,000; 2025 = $235,000 + $345,000 + $150,000 = $730,000. Liquidity 2024 = $640,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.60; 2025 = $730,000 ÷ $425,000 = 1.72. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($640,000 − $210,000) ÷ $400,000 = $430,000 ÷ $400,000 = 1.08; 2025 = ($730,000 − $235,000) ÷ $425,000 = $495,000 ÷ $425,000 = 1.16.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved modestly. The 2025 liquidity figure rose from 1.60 to 1.72, meaning current assets cover current liabilities more comfortably, helped by cash rising from $110,000 to $150,000 and current liabilities rising only from $400,000 to $425,000. The stricter liquidity measure, which excludes inventories, improved from 1.08 to 1.16, so short-term solvency does not depend on selling stock — important while HRI services a $1,200,000 bank loan and funds a $1,800,000 refurbishment. However, trade receivables rose from $320,000 to $345,000, tying up cash, and inventories rose from $210,000 to $235,000; if function and wedding event organisers pay late, the stronger ratios could deteriorate. The rise in liabilities also shows HRI is leaning more on short-term credit, so working capital discipline matters during the six-inn refit.

Conclusion: HRI's financial position has improved, though only gradually. Both the 2024-to-2025 liquidity measures (1.60 to 1.72, and 1.08 to 1.16) show stronger short-term solvency, and the improvement does not rest on inventory. The main residual risks are rising receivables and growing current liabilities, so HRI should tighten deposit terms on events and functions while the terraces open, and keep kitchen waste at or below 9.5% of prep weight to free cash for the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether HRI's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for HRI of introducing locally sourced riverside menus across its nine inns.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Locally sourced menus match the preferences of the 55% of 700 surveyed diners willing to pay up to $8 more per head, allowing HRI to charge a premium that protects its $57.00 contribution per unit even as food and beverage input costs rise 13.1%. They also appeal to the 46% who check ingredient provenance, strengthening HRI's brand, supporting the 4.2-out-of-5 review average, and helping the six refurbished terraces win destination-dining listings.

Disadvantage: Local sourcing can cost more than bulk wholesale supply and is seasonal and weather-dependent, which would increase the $38 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the $8 premium is accepted across the menu. Any supplier failure or inconsistency (for example shortages of local fish or unreliable delivery days) would also threaten the 27-per-month complaint rate HRI has worked down, and could undermine the terraces' relaunch promise of reliable riverside dining.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to HRI's research data, costs and terrace relaunch.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase to $13.09 per hour, and the 13.1% rise in food and beverage input costs will affect HRI. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If HRI's $1,200,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by about 0.75%, adding roughly $9,000 a year to financing costs and slightly raising fixed costs above $1,140,000. Higher rates may also make consumers more cautious about discretionary dining, though consumer spending on eating out still grew 2.6%, and HRI can shield itself by negotiating a fixed rate or paying down the loan from the $600,000 share-issue proceeds.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.09 per hour): With 230 employees, mainly kitchen and service roles, the rise lifts the whole wage bill. Roughly 45 kitchen porters and cleaners at or near minimum wage, each working about 1,800 hours a year, would see about $13.09 × 1,800 × 6.4% ≈ $1,510 extra a year per worker, or roughly $68,000 across those roles — though HRI can offset part through productivity gains of 113 units per worker (26,000 units ÷ 230 staff).

Input cost inflation (13.1% food and beverage): HRI's $38 variable cost is dominated by food, roughly $24 per room-night equivalent. A 13.1% rise on that portion adds about $3.14 per unit; at 26,000 units that is roughly $81,600 a year, cutting contribution per unit from $57.00 toward $53.86 and reducing profit, though HRI can partially recover through the $8 locally sourced premium menu and tighter waste control below the current 9.5% of prep weight.

Conclusion: The 13.1% rise in food and beverage input costs will have the greatest impact. It directly and repeatedly erodes the $57.00 contribution on every one of the 26,000 units sold, totalling roughly $81,600 a year, comfortably above the minimum-wage effect of roughly $68,000 across the lowest-paid cohort, and far above the $9,000 interest-rate increase. The minimum wage increase is the second most serious risk, while the interest-rate rise is smallest and can be managed by fixing the loan rate; all three still require HRI to review menu pricing before the April wage change.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to HRI.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on HRI's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of HRI with a well-justified judgement that food input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
